chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Sayf ibn 'Amirah from Sa'd al-Iskaf from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said:

A young man from the Ansar faced a woman in Medina, and the women used to wear their scarves behind their ears. So he looked at her while she was coming towards him. When she passed by, he continued looking at her as she entered an alleyway which had been named by the Clan of so-and-so. He kept looking behind her, and a bone in the wall or a piece of glass struck his face and cut it. When the woman went away, he looked and saw that blood was flowing onto his chest and his garment. So he said, 'By Allah, I will surely go to the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) and inform him.'

He said: So he came to him. When the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) saw him, he said to him, 'What is this?' So he informed him. Then Jibra'il (peace be upon him) descended with this Verse: 'Say to the believing men that they should cast down their looks and guard their private parts; that is purer for them; surely Allah is Aware of what they are doing.'
ai.seo_question: What is the origin of the Islamic ruling on lowering the gaze for men?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the causal link between the specific incident of the Ansari man’s prolonged gaze and the revelation of Surah An-Nur, 24:30, emphasizing the physical and spiritual consequences of unchecked looking. Shia scholars often cite this narrative to highlight the principle of 'cause of revelation' (sabab al-nuzul) while reinforcing the obligation of modesty for both genders, as the verse is followed by the command for women to lower their gaze in verse 31. The story serves as a practical reminder that the gaze is a gateway to desire, necessitating immediate vigilance to preserve chastity.
